# Weight gain in young chicks

In a feeding experiment, 50 chicks were weighed repeatedly from hatching to three weeks of age. Each chick received one of four diets. We begin with two questions about growth across all four groups. What shape does the population mean trajectory follow? How much do individual chicks differ in the way they grow?

# Setup and data

Create a `week4` folder, save your script as `lab7.R` there, and set it as your working directory. The `ChickWeight` dataset comes with R. Install the analysis packages with `pak` if needed, as in [Lab 1](BLR_lab_center_fixed.html#install-pak-once).

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| eval: false
library(pak)
pkg_install(c("ggplot2", "lmerTest"))
```

```{r}
#| label: read-chicks
#| output: true
library(ggplot2)
library(lmerTest)

chicks <- as.data.frame(datasets::ChickWeight)
head(chicks)
```

Each row gives the weight in grams of one chick at one age. `Chick` identifies the chick and `Time` gives its age in days since hatching.

# Explore the observed growth trajectories

Before choosing a model for growth, we can look at how the chicks gain weight over the three weeks. Following each chick over time lets us see how its growth compares with the average.

```{r}
#| label: observed-growth
#| output: true
ggplot(chicks, aes(Time, weight)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = Chick), color = "grey60", alpha = 0.55) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 1.2,
               color = "#175C65") +
  labs(x = "Age (days)", y = "Weight (g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Each grey line follows one chick. The darker line joins the mean weights of the chicks observed at each age.

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 1"}
What shape does the mean trajectory follow? How similar are the chicks at hatching, and how similar are the shapes of their trajectories as they grow?
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Model answer 1"}
Mean weight increases from about 41 g at hatching to 219 g on day 21. The increase is smaller over the first few days and becomes steeper. Chicks start close together and fan out. Some gain little weight while others gain rapidly, and the amount of curvature also appears to vary.
:::

# Fit a linear population mean growth trajectory

We start with age in days, the unit recorded at each weighing. We use day 10, near the middle of the study, as the reference age. Subtracting 10 from `Time` gives `day_c`: day 10 has `day_c = 0` and day 11 has `day_c = 1`. If $t_{ij}$ is the number of days from day 10 at weighing $i$ of chick $j$, the straight-line model is

$$
Y_{ij} = (\beta_0+b_{0j}) + \beta_1 t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}.
$$

The fixed intercept is the population mean weight on day 10. The random intercept shifts that trajectory up or down for each chick. All chicks share the same expected weight gain per day.

```{r}
#| label: linear-growth
#| output: true
chicks$day_c <- chicks$Time - 10
model_linear <- lmer(weight ~ day_c + (1 | Chick), data = chicks)
summary(model_linear)
```

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 2"}
Under the linear model, what is the estimated population mean weight on day 10? What daily weight gain does it predict for a given chick?
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Model answer 2"}
The estimated mean weight on day 10 is 115.1 g. The fitted line increases by 8.7 g per day. A chick's random intercept changes its expected weight on day 10 and the same shift applies at every age.
:::

# Check the shape of the mean trajectory

How well does a straight line describe mean growth over the three weeks? At each weighing we can compare the chick’s observed weight with the weight predicted for that chick. The difference is its conditional residual.

```{r}
#| label: linear-residuals
#| fig-alt: "Straight-line model. Mean residuals are positive near hatching and day 21 and negative around day 10."
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| output: true
chicks$residual_linear <- resid(model_linear)

ggplot(chicks, aes(Time, residual_linear)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, color = "#173F48") +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 1,
               color = "#C57722") +
  labs(x = "Age (days)", y = "Conditional residual (g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

The orange line joins the mean residuals at each age. Where it lies above zero, the model underestimates mean weight. Where it lies below zero, the model overestimates it.

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 3"}
Follow the orange line from hatching to day 21. At which ages does the straight-line model underestimate or overestimate mean weight? What shape would let the fitted trajectory follow this pattern?
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Model answer 3"}
At hatching the mean residual is about +13 g. Around day 10 it is −7 g, and by day 21 it is +6 g. The fitted line underestimates mean weight at the beginning and end and overestimates it in the middle. This pattern suggests allowing the mean curve to bend upwards.
:::

## Add a quadratic age term

A quadratic term lets the expected gain over a day depend on the chick’s age. We add $\beta_2 t_{ij}^2$ to the population mean trajectory, keeping the linear term and the same random intercept. In the model formula, `I(day_c^2)` squares the centered age.

```{r}
#| label: quadratic-growth
#| output: true
model_quadratic <- update(model_linear, . ~ . + I(day_c^2))
summary(model_quadratic)
```

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 4"}
In the fixed-effects table, what are the estimated coefficient and p-value for `I(day_c^2)`? What does the sign of the coefficient tell you about daily weight gain as the chicks grow older? How much evidence is there for including this term?
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Model answer 4"}
The estimated quadratic coefficient is 0.151 g/day². Its positive sign means the fitted mean trajectory bends upward. The chicks gain more weight per day, on average, as they grow older. The p-value is $3.46 \times 10^{-7}$, providing strong evidence for including curvature in the mean trajectory.
:::

Now plot the conditional residuals from the quadratic model. Compare the orange line with the one from the straight-line model.

```{r}
#| label: quadratic-residuals
#| fig-alt: "Quadratic model. Mean residuals stay close to zero across ages."
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| output: true
chicks$residual_quadratic <- resid(model_quadratic)

ggplot(chicks, aes(Time, residual_quadratic)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, color = "#173F48") +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 1,
               color = "#C57722") +
  labs(x = "Age (days)", y = "Conditional residual (g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 5"}
How does the pattern in the mean residuals change when the quadratic term is included? Looking back at the individual trajectories, what differences among chicks does a random intercept allow?
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Model answer 5"}
The mean residual now stays within about 3.4 g of zero at every age. The quadratic term captures the upward bend in the mean trajectory. A random intercept lets a chick stay consistently above or below that curve. In the observed plot, some chicks also gain weight faster or show more curvature than others.
:::

# Differences in growth between chicks

So far, every chick’s fitted curve has the same shape. A random intercept allows one chick to be heavier than another by the same amount at every age. The observed trajectories suggest two further ways in which chicks might differ. Some curves are steeper around day 10, and some bend more sharply over the following days. We can explore these possibilities while keeping the same quadratic population mean trajectory throughout.

We first give each chick its own linear slope. The term `(1 + day_c | Chick)` allows chicks to differ in weight and steepness at day 10 and estimates the correlation between the two. The mean trajectory is still quadratic.

```{r}
#| label: random-slope-days
#| output: true
#| warning: true
model_random_slope_days <- lmer(weight ~ day_c + I(day_c^2) +
                           (1 + day_c | Chick), data = chicks)
summary(model_random_slope_days)
```

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 6"}
Read the last lines of `summary(model_random_slope_days)`, below the coefficient tables. What warning does R report about convergence? Compare `max|grad|` with the tolerance (`tol`) in that message.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Model answer 6"}
R reports “Model failed to converge”. The reported gradient is about 0.0059, above the tolerance of 0.002.
:::

The model fitted in days triggers a convergence warning. R returns coefficient estimates, but the gradient at those estimates exceeds the tolerance used to check that the fit has reached the optimum. To investigate, we refit the same model with age in weeks. At day 21, centered age is 11 days and its square is 121. Expressed in weeks from the same reference age, those values are about 1.57 and 2.47. Working with these smaller values can help the fitting algorithm.

## The same model in weeks

Dividing `day_c` by 7 keeps day 10 at zero and changes the unit to one week. Both the fixed and random age terms use the new unit. Refit the model and check whether the convergence warning from Question 6 appears again.

```{r}
#| label: random-slope-weeks
#| output: true
chicks$week_c <- chicks$day_c / 7
model_random_slope_weeks <- lmer(weight ~ week_c + I(week_c^2) +
                      (1 + week_c | Chick), data = chicks)
summary(model_random_slope_weeks)
```

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 7"}
Does R still report a convergence warning when age is measured in weeks? Compare the last lines of the two model summaries.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Model answer 7"}
The convergence warning has cleared. The summary for the model fitted in days ends with a gradient warning. The summary for the refit in weeks ends after the fixed-effect correlations, with no convergence warning.
:::

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 8"}
How do the estimated mean weight and slope at day 10 compare across the two models once you convert the daily slope to grams per week?
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Model answer 8"}
Both intercepts give a mean weight of 108.19 g because zero still represents day 10. The estimated slope at that age is 8.34 g per day. Multiplying by seven gives about 58.4 g per week, matching the weekly model. Both coefficients describe the same steepness at day 10.
:::

## Comparing a common slope with chick-specific slopes

In Week 3, you interpreted the random-slope SD alongside the population slope. Here, the estimated mean growth rate at day 10 is 58.4 g/week, with a between-chick SD of 25.8 g/week. We can use AIC to assess whether the improvement in fit justifies allowing each chick its own slope.

Refit the common-slope model with age in weeks. Both models now use the same weighings, the same quadratic fixed effects and a random intercept for each chick. This lets us compare their AIC values using restricted maximum likelihood (REML), the default in `lmer()`.

```{r}
#| label: slope-comparison
#| output: true
model_common_slope_weeks <- lmer(weight ~ week_c + I(week_c^2) +
                                   (1 | Chick), data = chicks)
AIC(model_common_slope_weeks, model_random_slope_weeks)
```

**Akaike’s information criterion (AIC)** balances model fit against the number of estimated parameters. Pass the fitted model objects to `AIC()`, separated by commas. With one model, R returns its AIC value. With two or more, it prints one row per model in the order you supplied them.

In the table, `df` is the number of parameters estimated by each model. Compare the values in the `AIC` column. The model with the lower value is favored. Swapping the two model names reverses the rows and gives each model exactly the same score.

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 9"}
Which model does AIC favor for these chicks: a common slope at day 10 or a chick-specific slope?
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Model answer 9"}
AIC falls from 5596.9 for the common-slope model to 4738.6 for the chick-specific slope model. The improvement in fit outweighs the penalty for estimating the slope variance and its correlation with the random intercept. We carry the chick-specific slopes forward.
:::

## Adding a random quadratic slope

The selected model allows chicks to differ in steepness at day 10 while sharing the same curvature. Adding `I(week_c^2)` inside the parentheses for `Chick` lets curvature vary between chicks as well. With all three random coefficients in the same term, R estimates all three correlations among them.

```{r}
#| label: random-growth
#| output: true
#| message: true
#| warning: true
model_correlated_curvature <- lmer(weight ~ week_c + I(week_c^2) +
                     (1 + week_c + I(week_c^2) | Chick), data = chicks)
summary(model_correlated_curvature)
```

::: {.callout-important icon=false title="Question 10"}
Read the last lines of `summary(model_correlated_curvature)`. What message does R print immediately below the optimizer’s convergence code?
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Model answer 10"}
R reports `boundary (singular) fit` below the optimizer’s convergence code.
:::

In this model, a *singular fit* means the data support only two independent ways for the fitted curves to vary. Weight at day 10, growth rate at day 10 and curvature are so closely linked that knowing two almost determines the third.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false title="Optional: How similar hatching weights can link the random effects"}
At hatching, all 50 chicks weighed between 39 and 43 g. Imagine that every fitted curve started at exactly 41 g. If we knew a chick’s growth rate at day 10 and its curvature, we could trace how much weight it gained over those ten days. That would determine its weight at day 10. The chicks’ similar hatching weights may help explain the singular fit.
:::

For this lab, we retain `model_random_slope_weeks`, the model with a random intercept and a random linear slope. Chicks can differ in weight and growth rate at day 10, while their fitted curves share the same curvature.
